article.title: Bloated Military Budget
article.author: Matthew Hoh
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The United States can always find money for war. But when Americans need healthcare, education, housing, or investments in their communities, the familiar refrain is that there simply isn't enough money. That contradiction framed Our Bloated Military Budget , a session at the 2026 Left Coast Forum, held October 2–4 at California State University, Los Angeles. Featuring military veteran and peace advocate Matthew Hoh and foreign policy analyst Ben Freeman , the discussion examined the human and moral consequences of American militarism and the political culture that allows it to continue. Freeman, director of the Democratizing Foreign Policy program at the Quincy Institute, is co-author with William Hartung of The Trillion Dollar War Machine: How Runaway Military Spending Drives America into Foreign Wars and Bankrupts Us at Home . Hoh, a former Marine Corps officer and State Department official who resigned in protest of the Afghanistan War in 2009, brought a deeply personal perspective to the discussion. Rather than focusing exclusively on Pentagon expenditures, the conversation explored something more fundamental: What does perpetual warfare do to the people who fight it, the communities caught in its path, and the society that finances it? The War Comes Home Hoh began by describing the consequences of his military service, which continue nearly two decades after his final deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan. He spoke candidly about traumatic brain injury, psychological suffering, substance abuse, and the effects of medications prescribed to treat his conditions. His weight, he explained, had fluctuated dramatically over the years. But these physical struggles represented only part of the damage. Hoh described the concept of moral injury —the psychological and spiritual suffering that can arise when individuals participate in actions that violate their deepest ethical convictions. Unlike physical wounds, moral injury can be invisible, even while fundamentally altering a person's relationship with themselves and the world. Hoh argued that the connection between combat, guilt, and suicide among veterans receives insufficient attention, particularly when discussing the consequences of killing. He recalled undergoing years of Veterans Affairs therapy without being asked directly about his participation in wartime violence. For Hoh, this omission reflects a larger institutional reluctance to confront what warfare actually requires of those sent to fight. Related: 9/11, Blowback, and the History America Refuses to Discuss "War Makes You Its Agent" One of the discussion's most powerful moments centered on Hoh's observation that "war makes you its agent." He explained that many service members enter combat believing they can retain control over their moral choices. They imagine that they will act conscientiously, protect civilians, and avoid participating in atrocities. But warfare, Hoh argued, operates according to forces that overwhelm individual intentions. To illustrate his point, he referenced a scene from the television series Generation Kill , in which Marines attempt to avoid shooting innocent civilians by firing a warning smoke grenade toward an approaching vehicle. The grenade accidentally strikes and kills an elderly man. Even an attempt to prevent violence produces another death. For Hoh, the lesson was unmistakable: Individuals cannot reliably control the consequences of their actions within the machinery of war. His reflections also challenged the conventional American distinction between heroic soldiers and the people designated as enemies. In Iraq and Afghanistan, he argued, many of those fighting American forces were resisting foreign military occupation. "We invaded them. We occupied them," he said, emphasizing that American intervention helped create the very resistance it then sought to defeat. The People Left Behind Hoh's account became particularly poignant when he described the Iraqis with whom he had worked during the occupation. Among them was Mona, an Iraqi woman who helped care for the American personnel and became something of a mother figure to him. Hoh has a tattoo honoring her. He does not know what happened to Mona after he left Iraq. He similarly lost contact with other Iraqi colleagues, including a deputy whose community was devastated by the Islamic State. These relationships remain central to his understanding of his responsibilities as a veteran and peace advocate. Hoh acknowledged that much of his activism is driven by anger and guilt. He feels an obligation to speak for people whose suffering has been forgotten or dismissed, while those responsible for devastating wars have largely escaped accountability. His white poppy, which commemorates all victims of war rather than only military personnel, symbolizes that commitment. The suffering of American veterans, he emphasized, cannot be separated from the much greater devastation experienced by populations subjected to American military intervention. Why Doesn't America Learn? Freeman raised a question that goes to the heart of antiwar organizing: How can the experiences of veterans and military families become part of the national conversation before another war begins? He described conversations with Gold Star mothers—women who had lost children in military service—and efforts to amplify their experiences as warnings against future military interventions. Hoh's response was sobering. "Every generation thinks they're exempt from history," he observed. Despite the repeated failures of American military interventions, each generation persuades itself that the next conflict will be different. Hoh recounted speaking with students enrolled in military officer training programs after his resignation from the State Department. Although some acknowledged his arguments, they continued into military service. Only afterward did some tell him that his warnings had been correct. Yet Hoh also identified a source of hope. Independent journalism, alternative media, and social platforms have weakened the ability of political and military elites to monopolize public understanding of war. This changing information environment, he suggested, gives opponents of militarism opportunities that earlier generations did not possess. A Military Machine That Cannot Stop The discussion also turned toward the dangers of confrontation with Iran and the possibility of nuclear escalation. Hoh warned about efforts to develop lower-yield nuclear weapons and promote the idea that nuclear war could be limited or controlled. He questioned whether American leaders fully appreciate the risks associated with the country's continuing nuclear modernization program. These dangers underscore the broader critique presented in the panel's description: The military-industrial complex is not merely a collection of weapons manufacturers. It is an interconnected system of political power, institutional interests, military infrastructure, and economic priorities that perpetuates warfare. Meanwhile, public investments are routinely subjected to austerity arguments that rarely constrain military spending. Related: American Way of War: A Required Reading List What Kind of Security Are We Buying? Ultimately, the panel challenged the assumption that ever-increasing military expenditures necessarily make Americans safer. A nation can possess extraordinary destructive power while leaving its own communities underfunded, its veterans struggling, and populations overseas devastated by wars undertaken in the name of national security. Hoh's testimony gave that contradiction a profoundly human dimension. Freeman's questions connected those individual experiences to the larger challenge of changing American foreign policy before another generation suffers the same consequences. The issue is not simply whether the United States spends too much on its military. It is whether a political system that consistently prioritizes warfare over human needs can genuinely claim to be protecting its people. The question Americans must confront is not whether we can afford peace, but how much longer we can afford the human, moral, and economic costs of endless war.
